add_divergence.description: Given a non-dendritic flow network and required attributes, adds a divergence attribute according to NHDPlus data model methods.
add_divergence.details:
When considering downstream connections with diversions, there are three factors considered to determine which is primary.
1a) same name
1b) is named
2) feature type (type_attr controls this)
3) flows to coast (has a coastal connection is preferred)

The following list describes the order of precedence for tests
1: 1a, 2, 3
2: 1a, 2
3: The NHDPlus uses diverted fraction this is not used currently.
4: 1b, 2, 3
5: 2, 3
6: 1b, 3
7: 3,
8: 1b, 2
9: 2
10: 1b

If all checks return and no primary connection has been identified, the connection with a smaller id is chosen.

In the case that there are two or more upstream connections, the upstream name to use is chosen 1) if there is only one upstream flowline with a name 2) if one of the upstream flowlines with a name matches the downstream line, 3) if one of the upstream flowlines is of a "major" type and others are not, and, 4) if no criteria exist to select one, the smallest id value otherwise.

add_divergence.value: returns x with a `divergence` attribute appended

arguments.hydro_locations: data.frame. Hydro locations to measure from, with `hydro_location_id`, `id` and `id_measure`, on `x` (for example the output of `get_confluences()`).
arguments.x: `hy_topo` or `hy_node`, or a data.frame coercible with `hy()`. Carries `aggregate_id` and `length_km`. A `topo_sort` column keeps building the aggregate flowpath axis cheap; without it a full topological sort is run.

add_hydro_location_distance.description:
Records each position as a signed distance along its aggregate flowpath from the nearest of a set of hydro locations, such as the confluences returned by `get_confluences()`. An aggregate flowpath is the run of flowlines that share an `aggregate_id` and link end to end, such as an identified mainstem. Each position is a flowline `id` and `id_measure`. The result adds the `aggregate_id` the position is on, the `hydro_location_id` it is measured from, and `distance_km`.

A distance from a confluence does not depend on the flowline ids of the network it was recorded on. `index_hydro_location_distance()` takes the same record and places it on any network that carries the same aggregate flowpaths, for example to move a gage location from NHDPlusV2 to 3DHP. The placed position is approximate in absolute terms, since the receiving network puts the confluence at its own spot, but it stays on the same side of the confluence.
add_hydro_location_distance.details:
Positions and hydro locations are converted to kilometers along the aggregate flowpath axis (the aggregate flowpath measured from its downstream end in `x`). Only hydro locations on the same `aggregate_id` as a position are candidates, and the one with the smallest absolute difference in kilometers is recorded. A position exactly halfway between two hydro locations takes the one with the smaller `hydro_location_id`, compared as strings.

`distance_km` is negative when the position is downstream of the hydro location (toward the outlet) and positive when it is upstream (toward the headwater). The sign is a hydroloom convention; HY_DistanceDescription in HY_Features describes the same two directions as downstream and upstream.

sections.Measures: `id_measure` is an interpolative measure along a single flowline: a percent of the line from its outlet, 0 at the outlet (downstream end) and 100 at the inlet (upstream, head end).

add_hydro_location_distance.value: `indexes` with `aggregate_id`, `hydro_location_id` and `distance_km` added. `aggregate_id` is `NA` for a position on a flowline without one. A position on an aggregate flowpath with no hydro location gets `NA` `hydro_location_id` and `distance_km`, with a message.

add_levelpaths.description:
Assigns level paths using the stream-leveling approach of NHD and NHDPlus. If arbolate sum is provided in the weight column, this will match the behavior of NHDPlus. Any numeric value can be included in this column and the largest value will be followed when no nameid is available.

x must include id, toid, and conditionally divergence attributes. If a "topo_sort" (hydrosequence in nhdplus terms) attribute is included, it will be used instead of recreation.
add_levelpaths.details:
The levelpath algorithm defines upstream mainstem paths through a network. At a given junction with two or more upstream flowlines, the main path is either 1) the path with the same name, 2) the path with any name, 3) or the path with the larger weight. If the `weight_attribute` is `override_factor` times larger on a path, it will be followed regardless of the name_attribute indication.

If id and toid are non-dendritic so id:toid is many to one and id is non-unique, a divergence attribute must be included such that the dendritic network can be extracted after the network is sorted.

add_measures.description:
given a set of connected flowlines that have ids and aggregate ids, adds from_aggregate_id_measure and to_aggregate_id_measure for use with index_points_to_lines

Aggregate ids, such as mainstem ids or reachcodes span multiple flowlines. Linear referencing along these features requires knowledge of the portion of the aggregate line a given flowline makes up. This function assumes that the complete aggregate feature is included and calculates the measure of the top and bottom of each flowline along each aggregate line.
add_measures.details:
If no "toid" attribute is included, make_attribute_topology is used to to create one. This is required to ensure the flowlines making up each aggregate line are sorted in a known upstream to downstream order.

This function assumes that all flowlines that make up an aggregate feature are included. Returned measures will be incomplete and incorrect if aggregate features (mainstems of reaches) are truncated.

add_measures.value: x with aggregate measures added to it

Adds a return divergence attribute to the provided network. The method implemented matches that of the NHDPlus except in the rare case that a diversion includes more than one secondary path.

See add_divergence and make_node_topology.
add_return_divergence.details:

All network connections with more than one downstream feature are considered.

check_hy_graph.description: check that a network graph doesn't contain cycles and, optionally, that its divergence attributes are internally consistent.
check_hy_graph.details:
For `divergence_check`: `id`, `fromnode`, `divergence` and, conditionally, `divergence_fraction`.

The divergence check enforces the attribute contract that `accumulate_downstream()` documents and depends on: 0 indicates a catchment that is not downstream of a divergence, 1 the primary path downstream of a divergence, and 2 a diverted path. Total upstream routing needs a complete and consistent `divergence` attribute to avoid double counting through systems of diverted channels. Use `add_divergence()` to derive the attribute where it is absent.

Divergence checks, grouping features by shared `fromnode`:

1. `divergence` is populated and in `{0, 1, 2}`.
2. Every node with more than one outgoing feature has exactly one `divergence == 1`.
3. No `divergence == 0` on a node with more than one outgoing feature.
4. No `divergence` of 1 or 2 on a node with a single outgoing feature.

A node may have any number of diverted paths, so more than one `divergence == 2` at a node is valid and is not flagged.

When a `divergence_fraction` attribute is present, three further checks apply:

1. `divergence_fraction` is populated and in `[0, 1]`.
2. `divergence_fraction` sums to 1 across each `fromnode` group.
3. No `divergence == 2` feature takes the entire flow.

A cycle is a set of flowlines in which water leaving any one of them can, by following `toid`, return to it: the strongly connected components of the `id` to `toid` graph that hold more than one flowline, plus any flowline whose `toid` is its own `id`. Every network is checked for cycles.
check_hy_graph.title: Check hy Graph
check_hy_graph.value: if no problems are found, returns TRUE. If problems are found, problem rows. Rows returned by the divergence check carry a `divergence_issue` column naming the failed checks. Rows returned by the cycle check are every row whose `id` and `toid` lie on a common cycle, in input order, with `component` (which cycle, numbered from 1 in byte order of each cycle's least identifier compared as text) and `reciprocal` (`TRUE` when the cycle has exactly two flowlines). Checks run in order and the first one to find a problem returns, so a single call reports one class of problem at a time.

get_confluences.description:
Returns a hydro location for each confluence where one aggregate flowpath flows into another, such as a tributary mainstem joining the mainstem it drains to. An aggregate flowpath is the run of flowlines that share an `aggregate_id` and link end to end. Each confluence is identified by the tributary's `aggregate_id` and placed on the first flowline of the receiving aggregate flowpath below it.

Confluences work as reference points for distances along a river because any network that carries both mainstems has the confluence too. Pass the result to `add_hydro_location_distance()` to record positions as distances from these confluences, and to `index_hydro_location_distance()` to place those distances on the same or another network.
get_confluences.details:
A confluence is found where the bottom flowline of one aggregate flowpath connects downstream to a flowline with a different `aggregate_id`. The hydro location goes at the upstream end (`id_measure` 100) of that downstream flowline rather than at the end of the tributary. That keeps it on the receiving aggregate flowpath, and it still exists when the receiving flowpath is truncated just above the confluence. Only topology is used; no coordinates are read.

Each aggregate flowpath has one bottom flowline, so it yields at most one confluence. A tributary whose downstream connection is a diversion (`divergence == 2`) is dropped with a warning.

The output follows the `hydrolocation` feature type of OGC 25-045, with `aggregate_id` in the role of `mainstem_id` and `hydro_location_id` in the role of `link`.

sections.Measures: `id_measure` is an interpolative measure along a single flowline: a percent of the line from its outlet, 0 at the outlet (downstream end) and 100 at the inlet (upstream, head end).

get_subpath.description:
Returns the subpath between two positions on one aggregate flowpath. An aggregate flowpath is the run of flowlines that share an `aggregate_id` and link end to end, such as an identified mainstem. A subpath is the part of it between two positions, each given as a flowline `id` and `id_measure`. The result lists the flowlines of the subpath from downstream to upstream, with the two end flowlines cut at the positions' measures. This is how to pull a stretch of river, such as the river between a gage and a confluence, out of any network that carries `aggregate_id`.

Both positions must be on the same aggregate flowpath. A stretch that crosses a confluence of two mainstems takes two calls, one for each mainstem, split at the confluence.

Support for cross-aggregate_id paths may be included in a future release.
get_subpath.details:
`from` and `to` can be given in either order. Each position is converted to kilometers along the aggregate flowpath axis (the aggregate flowpath measured from its downstream end in `x`), and the subpath covers the kilometer span between the two. Pieces always come back downstream to upstream. If a `from` position is upstream of its `to`, `reversed` is `TRUE` on every row for that pair.

`snap_m` keeps small offsets from cutting slivers. An end within `snap_m` meters of a flowline boundary moves to that boundary before cutting, so a node a few meters inside a flowline does not leave a sliver, and two source flowlines that share a node share one cut. Zero-length pieces are dropped. If both ends land on one point after snapping, the result for that `line_id` is a single row with an `NA` `id` and zero `length_km`.

When `x` is `sf` and lwgeom is installed, each piece's geometry is cut with `lwgeom::st_linesubstring()` and attached.

hy.description:
Renames each column hydroloom knows by another name to its standard hydroloom name, as `COMID` becomes `id` and `ToCOMID` becomes `toid`. The vocabulary, the list of standard names and the source names known for each, ships with the package as `hy_vocab.json`. When two columns could take one name, the column whose source name comes later in the vocabulary takes it, with a warning, and the other keeps its input name. A `permanent_identifier` column keeps its name whenever another column could take the same name. Other columns keep their input names and values.

Each identifier column takes one identifier type, and each flag column coded 1/0 becomes `TRUE`/`FALSE`. In R, that type is integer when the column, with its partner if it has one (`toid` for `id`, `tonode` for `fromnode`), holds only whole numbers within the 32-bit integer range, and text when either holds larger whole numbers or text. In Python, every column the vocabulary types as an identifier (`id`, `toid`, `fromnode`, `tonode`, `levelpath`, and others) becomes text (`str`). A missing `toid` becomes the value that marks an outlet (a flowline that flows to nothing else in the table), `""` when identifiers are text. In R, that value is `0` when identifiers are integer. A table with geometry keeps its geometry column, moved to the last position. In R, that column is renamed `geom`. `hy_network_type()` reports which network layout the result follows, such as an id/toid list or a fromnode/tonode list.
hy.title: Align a table with hydroloom names and types
hy.value: the input table with hydroloom names and types, keeping its geometry when it has one. In R, the result is a `hy` object whose S3 class is the most specific hydroloom subclass its columns fit, such as `hy_topo` or `hy_node`.

arguments.x: object to query.
arguments.include_conversions: logical. If TRUE, also marks functions reachable via a single representation conversion.

hy_capabilities.description:
Returns a data.frame indicating which hydroloom functions can operate on the input object given its current representation and columns.

Functions marked TRUE are directly callable. In R, use `include_conversions = TRUE` to see what becomes available after a single representation conversion.
hy_capabilities.title: What operations are available for this network?
hy_capabilities.value: data.frame with one row per function and columns `function` (character), `available` (logical), and `via` (character: the one conversion function that makes an unavailable function callable, `""` when the function is directly callable or no single conversion reaches it).

hy_flownetwork.description:
A `hy_flownetwork` object is a junction table — a non-dendritic edge list of `id` and `toid` rows where `id` may repeat. Each row records one connection between an upstream catchment or flowline and a downstream one, and optional `upmain`/`downmain` logical columns annotate which of the connections at a divergence is the main path. This is the only edge-list-shaped representation in hydroloom that preserves divergences directly.

Unlike the other class pages on this index, `hy_flownetwork` does **not** inherit from `hy` — `id` is not guaranteed to be a primary key, and a `hy_flownetwork` passes `is.hy()` only when it carries `orig_names`. The user-facing producer `to_flownetwork()` drops the `orig_names` round-trip metadata that `hy` carries; a `hy_flownetwork` produced by `hy()` or `classify_hy()` from a non-dendritic data.frame may still have `orig_names` attached internally so name-aligned dispatch can restore the user's column names on return.
hy_flownetwork.details:
`hy_flownetwork` is what hydroloom's internal classifier produces (via `hy()`) when an `id`/`toid` table has duplicated `id` values, and what `to_flownetwork()` produces from a `hy_leveled` input. The `upmain`/`downmain` annotation, when present, lets divergence-aware operations choose a main path without having to re-derive it from levelpath identity each time.

Several hydroloom operations that were originally written against `hy_topo` accept `hy_flownetwork` directly through delegate methods, because the underlying algorithm already tolerates non-dendritic input: `add_streamorder()`, `accumulate_downstream()`, `get_bridge_flowlines()`, `add_levelpaths()`, and `make_node_topology()` all work on `hy_flownetwork` without conversion.

- Delegated to the `hy_topo` algorithm: `add_streamorder()`, `accumulate_downstream()`, `get_bridge_flowlines()`, `add_levelpaths()`, `make_node_topology()`

Going the other direction — from `hy_node` or `hy_leveled` into `hy_flownetwork` — is what `to_flownetwork()` is for.

hy_leveled.description:
A `hy_leveled` object is a `hy_topo` carrying the additional columns produced by stream leveling: `topo_sort`, `levelpath`, and `levelpath_outlet_id`. These columns are what mainstem-aware operations (Pfafstetter coding, stream level, junction-table conversion) need in order to run.

`hy_leveled` is a strict subclass of `hy_topo`, so every function that accepts a `hy_topo` accepts a `hy_leveled` as well.
hy_leveled.details:
`hy_leveled` exists to mark a `hy_topo` as having been through `add_levelpaths()` so downstream functions can dispatch on the presence of leveling without re-checking column names. The leveling columns encode mainstem path identity (`levelpath`), the outlet that closes that path (`levelpath_outlet_id`), and the topological order along the network (`topo_sort`).

Like `hy_topo`, `hy_leveled` requires unique `id` and cannot represent divergences as duplicated rows. Convert to hy_flownetwork via `to_flownetwork()` to preserve main and diverted paths in junction-table form.

hy_node.description:
A `hy_node` object is a bipartite graph over catchments or flowlines and nexuses: each catchment (or flowline) is one row, carrying a `fromnode` (the upstream nexus it leaves) and a `tonode` (the downstream nexus it enters). Connectivity is recovered by matching `tonode` to `fromnode` across rows. This is the representation that natively supports divergences without duplicating rows — a divergence is simply a nexus with more than one outgoing feature.

As with `hy_topo`, a `hy_node` represents either a catchment topology or a flowline topology. Catchments carry a known local drainage area and are 1:1 with their flowpaths; flowlines are linear features without a committed local drainage area. The two graphs are practically related but functionally distinct.

`hy_node` inherits from `hy`.
hy_node.details:
Because divergences are encoded through shared node identifiers rather than row duplication, `hy_node` requires unique `id` even on non-dendritic networks. The `fromnode`/`tonode` pair carries the connectivity that an `id`/`toid` edge list cannot.

`hy_node` is the entry point for hydroloom's divergence-aware operations: `add_divergence()` flags main and diverted paths from geometry, `add_return_divergence()` marks where diverted paths return to the main, and `subset_network()` walks the bipartite graph during subsetting.

hy_topo.description:
A `hy_topo` object is a self-referencing edge list representing either a catchment topology or a flowline topology: one row per feature, carrying an `id` and a `toid` that points at the immediately downstream feature. This is the main representation for downstream traversal, topological sorting, and most accumulation algorithms in hydroloom.

Catchment topology and flowline topology are functionally separate graphs. A catchment carries a known local drainage area and is 1:1 with its flowpath (the linear realization of the catchment). A flowline is a linear feature without a committed local drainage area — it may coincide with a catchment's flowpath, but that relationship is not guaranteed. `hy_topo` represents either graph; the two are practically related but should not be conflated.

`hy_topo` inherits from `hy`. The enriched subclass `hy_leveled` extends `hy_topo` with topo-sort and levelpath columns, so methods written for `hy_topo` apply to `hy_leveled` objects without modification.
hy_topo.details:
`hy_topo` requires unique `id`. A divergence would need two downstream connections from the same upstream feature — that is, two rows with the same `id` — and `hy_topo` does not permit that. Networks with divergences belong in hy_node (a bipartite graph through `fromnode`/`tonode`) or in hy_flownetwork (a junction table that annotates main and diverted paths). When the internal classifier called from `hy()` sees a duplicated `id` in an `id`/`toid` table, it produces an `hy_flownetwork` rather than an `hy_topo`.

For the authoritative, programmatic view of which functions are callable on a particular object, use `hy_capabilities()`.

- Accumulation and traversal: `accumulate_downstream()`, `navigate_hydro_network()`, `navigate_network_dfs()`, `make_index_ids()`

- To hy_flownetwork (junction table): `add_levelpaths()` then `to_flownetwork()`

index_hydro_location_distance.description:
Places distances from hydro locations on the flowlines of `x`, the inverse of `add_hydro_location_distance()`. Each record gives an `aggregate_id`, a `hydro_location_id` and a `distance_km`, and the result adds the flowline `id` and `id_measure` at that distance. An aggregate flowpath is the run of flowlines that share an `aggregate_id` and link end to end, such as an identified mainstem.

Because a record points to a hydro location rather than to a flowline, `x` does not have to be the network the distance was recorded on. A distance recorded on NHDPlusV2 can be placed on 3DHP, as long as both carry the same `aggregate_id` values and `hydro_locations` is on `x`, for example `get_confluences(x)`.

A transferred position is approximate in absolute terms. `x` has unique flowlines and puts the hydro location at its own location along them, so `distance_km` laid out on `x` may not land at the same point on the ground as it did on the network it was recorded on. However, which side of the referenced hydro location the position is on is transfered intact. For a confluence that is what matters: crossing it changes the upstream drainage by a whole tributary basin, while moving along the mainstem between confluences changes it only by local drainage. Where a position has to be exact on `x`, index the original point on `x` instead. The mainstem referencing article shows a worked case: https://doi-usgs.github.io/hydroloom/articles/mainstem_referencing.html
index_hydro_location_distance.details:
Each record's hydro location is converted to kilometers along the aggregate flowpath axis of `x` (the aggregate flowpath measured from its downstream end), `distance_km` is added, and the flowline holding the result is found. A result that lands on a boundary between two flowlines goes to the lower one, at `id_measure` 100. `distance_km` uses the sign convention of `add_hydro_location_distance()`: negative downstream, positive upstream.

`status` reports what happened to each record. `placed` is a normal result. `hydro_location_not_in_x` means the `aggregate_id` and `hydro_location_id` pair is not in `hydro_locations`, or that hydro location is not on `x`, and `id` and `id_measure` are `NA`. `past_end` means the distance runs past the downstream or upstream end of the aggregate flowpath's flowlines in `x` (a truncated network, for example). arguments.x: data.frame. A table of flowlines or catchments; columns hydroloom knows by another name, from NHDPlusV2, NHDPlusHR, 3DHP, or elsewhere (such as NHDPlus `COMID`, `ToCOMID`), are renamed to hydroloom names first. In R, hydroloom_names gives the source names hydroloom knows.

index_points_to_lines.description: given an sf point geometry column, return id, aggregate_id (e.g. reachcode), and aggregate id measure for each point.
index_points_to_lines.details:
Note 1: Inputs are cast into LINESTRINGS. Because of this, the measure output of inputs that are true multipart lines may be in error.

Note 2: This algorithm finds the nearest node in the input flowlines to identify which flowline the point should belong to. As a second pass, it can calculate the measure to greater precision than the nearest flowline geometry node.

Note 3: Offset is returned in units consistent with the projection of the input points.

Note 4: See `dfMaxLength` input to sf::st_segmentize() for details of handling of precision parameter.

Note 5: "from" is downstream -- 0 is the outlet "to" is upstream -- 100 is the inlet

Note 6: This function does not assume that it has access to the complete aggregate feature. From and to aggregate id measures must be included for each flowline in order to have aggregate id measures (reachcode or mainstem measures) in the output.

make_index_ids.title: Make Index ids
make_index_ids.value:
index ids for mode "to" or "from": each flowline's neighbors as positions, the downstream flowlines for "to" and the upstream flowlines for "from", sorted by `id` as text, character by character (so "100" comes before "30"). In R, a "to" entry of 0 marks a `toid` outside the table and is not a position. When the table has `downmain` ("to") or `upmain` ("from"), each connection also says whether it is on the main path, the one that carries the same river on through a confluence or divergence. For mode "both", the "to" and then the "from" index ids.

In Python, the result's `uniques`, a pandas Index, gives the `id` at each position, as text, and its `indptr` and `indices` hold the neighbors: those of the flowline at position i are `indices[indptr[i]:indptr[i + 1]]`. Its `main` holds the main-path flag of each connection, aligned with `indices`, taken from `downmain` ("to") or `upmain` ("from"), and is `None` when the table has no such column.

In R, the value is a list containing named elements:

- to: adjacency matrix with columns that correspond to `unqiue(x$id)`
- lengths: vector indicating the number of connections from each node
- to_list: a data.frame with an `id`, `indid` and a `toindid` list column.

In R, the list has names `froms`, `lengths`, and `froms_list` for mode "from".

In R, the long_form output is deprecated and will be removed in a future release.

navigate_network_dfs.description: given a starting node, return all reachable paths. Once visited, a node is marked as visited and will not take part in a future path.
navigate_network_dfs.details:
`navigate_network_dfs` offers two usage patterns. In the simple case, you can provide an `hy` in which case preprocessing is performed automatically, or you can do the preprocessing ahead of time and provide index ids. The latter is more complicated but can be much faster in certain circumstances.

`hy` object:

If the function will only be called one or a few times, it can be called with `x` containing (at a minimum) `id` and `toid`. For "upmain" and "downmain" support, `x` also requires attributes for determination of the primary upstream and downstream connection across every junction.

In this pattern, the `hy` object will be passed to make_index_ids called for every call to `navigate_network_dfs` and the resulting index ids will be used for network navigation.

Index ids:

If the function will be called repeatedly or index_ids are available for other reasons, the index ids as created by make_index_ids ("to" mode for downstream or "from" mode for upstream). For "upmain" and "downmain" support, the index ids must include the main-path flag of each connection, `main`, which make_index_ids adds when the table has `downmain` ("to" mode) or `upmain` ("from" mode). In R, `main` is an element of the list.

rescale_measures.description:
Given an aggregate_id (e.g. reachcode in NHDPlus) measure and the from and to measure for an id (e.g. COMID flowline in NHDPlus), returns the measure along the id flowline. This is useful where many flowlines make up a single aggregate feature. "Measures" are typically referenced to the aggregate feature. Flowlines have a stated from-measure / to-measure. In some cases it is useful to rescale the measure such that it is relative only to the flowline.

from is downstream -- 0 is the outlet to is upstream -- 100 is the inlet

sort_network.description:
given a network with an id and and toid, returns a sorted and potentially split set of output. Sort is from top to bottom so traversing the response from top to bottom will go from upstream to downstream.

Can also be used as a very fast implementation of upstream with tributaries navigation. The full network from each outlet is returned in sorted order.

If a network includes diversions, all flowlines downstream of the diversion are visited prior to continuing upstream. See note on the `outlets` parameter for implications of this implementation detail.
sort_network.title: Sort Network
sort_network.value: data.frame containing a topologically sorted version of the requested network and optionally a terminal id.

subset_network.description:
Subsets a network to features upstream of a given outlet. For non-dendritic networks, the function identifies flowpaths connected to the upstream basin via fromnode/tonode that are not reachable by upstream navigation alone. This is useful for networks where an upstream navigation returns a basin that contains a nested basin (closed or intersecting) connected through diversions. If `only_up` is `FALSE`, those nested basins are captured by navigating downstream from missed diversions to find their outlets, then navigating upstream from those outlets.

Note: If a diversion leaves a basin entirely, the subset will include the entire basin upstream of where the diversion terminates. this function will return both closed basins and intersecting basins.

subset_network.value:
data.frame subset of `x` containing flowpaths upstream of the outlet.

Note: if "toid" is included in the input, it will be returned without modification. This may result in one or more "toid" entries that contain ids that are not part of the subset.
